title: SQL Project
text:
Overview
For this project, my partner and I designed and queried a relational database using data from NASA’s Exoplanet Archive. The goal of the project was to examine patterns in exoplanet discoveries, including how discovery methods have changed over time and which methods are responsible for the largest number of confirmed exoplanet discoveries.
The project involved cleaning CSV files, importing them into a DuckDB database, designing simplified relational tables, writing SQL queries, and creating visualizations in R.

title: SQL Project
section: Load Packages and Connect to Database
text:
Load Packages and Connect to Database

library(DBI)
library(duckdb)
library(readr)
library(tidyverse)


# Create a DuckDB database connection.
# This allows SQL queries to be run inside the Quarto document.
con_nasa <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), dbdir = "nasa_db")

title: SQL Project
text:
Accessing and Cleaning the Data

# Read in the original CSV files.
# The comment = "#" argument skips metadata/comment lines at the top of the files.
planet_data <- readr::read_csv("planet_data.csv", comment = "#")
planet_discovery <- readr::read_csv("planet_discovery.csv", comment = "#")
star_data <- readr::read_csv("star_data.csv", comment = "#")

# Save cleaned versions of the datasets so they can be imported into DuckDB.
readr::write_csv(planet_data, "planet_data_clean.csv")
readr::write_csv(planet_discovery, "planet_discovery_clean.csv")
readr::write_csv(star_data, "star_data_clean.csv")

title: SQL Project
SQL Project
text:
Database Design
The original NASA Exoplanet Archive data contained repeated measurements for some planets and host stars. To create cleaner tables for analysis, I grouped observations by planet name and host star, then summarized repeated measurements using averages or maximum values where appropriate.

-- Create a cleaned planets table.
-- Some planets appear more than once in the original data, so this table
-- groups by planet and host star and uses the average orbital period.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE planets AS
SELECT
  pl_name,
  hostname,
  AVG(pl_orbper) AS pl_orbper
FROM planet_data
WHERE pl_orbper IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY pl_name, hostname
ORDER BY pl_name;


-- Create a cleaned discoveries table.
-- DISTINCT removes duplicate rows, while the WHERE clause keeps only
-- planets with a recorded discovery year.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE discoveries AS
SELECT DISTINCT
  pl_name,
  discoverymethod,
  disc_year
FROM planet_discovery
WHERE disc_year IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY pl_name;


-- Create a cleaned stars table.
-- MAX(sy_pnum) keeps the maximum reported number of planets for each host star.
-- AVG(st_rad) and AVG(st_mass) take averages for repeated measurements of
-- stellar radius and mass
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE stars AS
SELECT
  hostname,
  MAX(sy_pnum) AS sy_pnum,
  AVG(st_rad) AS st_rad,
  AVG(st_mass) AS st_mass
FROM star_data
GROUP BY hostname
ORDER BY hostname;


-- Check that the cleaned tables were created successfully.
SHOW TABLES;

Examining Planet Discovery Patterns
In this section, I examined patterns in exoplanet discoveries and discovery methods over time.

Query 1

-- Count the number of planets discovered by each discovery method.
-- This helps identify which methods account for the most confirmed discoveries.
SELECT discoverymethod, COUNT(*) AS n_planets
FROM discoveries
GROUP BY discoverymethod
ORDER BY n_planets DESC;

The transit and radial velocity methods were responsible for the majority of planet discoveries. The transit method involves detecting changes in a star’s brightness when a planet passes in front of it, while the radial velocity method detects small movements in a star caused by the gravitational pull of orbiting planets.

-- Count the number of planets discovered in each year.
SELECT disc_year, COUNT(*) AS n_planets

Query 3

-- Join the planets and discoveries tables to compare average orbital period
-- by discovery method.
-- HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5 removes discovery methods with very small sample sizes.
SELECT d.discoverymethod,
       AVG(p.pl_orbper) AS avg_orbper,
       COUNT(*) AS n_planets
FROM planets AS p
JOIN discoveries AS d
  ON p.pl_name = d.pl_name
GROUP BY d.discoverymethod

title: Senior Research Project
text: For my senior research project, I examined whether early European carbon taxes reduced national CO₂ emissions per capita in the 5 years following their implementation. This project combined applied econometrics, environmental policy analysis, and data visualization to study how carbon tax adoption affected emissions across European countries before the introduction of the European Union Emissions Trading System.

title: Senior Research Project
text: For my senior research project, I examined whether early European carbon taxes reduced national CO₂ emissions per capita in the 5 years following their implementation. This project combined applied econometrics, environmental policy analysis, and data visualization to study how carbon tax adoption affected emissions across European countries before the introduction of the European Union Emissions Trading System.

title: Senior Research Project
text:
Research Question
Did early European carbon taxes reduce national CO₂ emissions per capita in the short run?

title: Senior Research Project
text:
Data
I used country-level panel data for 29 European countries from 1985 to 2004, with a final dataset containing 1,160 observations across 27 variables. The dataset included emissions data, carbon tax adoption timing, and economic and environmental controls such as GDP per capita and average annual temperature.

title: Senior Research Project
text:
Methods
To estimate the effects of carbon tax adoption, I used a Sun & Abraham event study framework with country and year fixed effects. This approach allowed me to compare emissions trends before and after carbon tax adoption while accounting for differences in adoption timing, inherent country differences, and shocks across time.

title: Senior Research Project
text:
Key Findings
The results suggested that early European carbon taxes did not lead to large or statistically significant short-run reductions in national CO₂ emissions per capita. This may be because the first taxes were much less intense than carbon taxes today. However, additional analysis suggested some evidence of modest shifts in fossil fuel energy use following adoption.

title: My R Package: knntuner
text:
knntuner is an R package I developed for my Advanced Data Computing course. The package is designed to streamline parts of the K-nearest neighbors modeling workflow in caret by helping users create tuning grids, define cross-validation settings, and identify the best-performing value of (k).
The goal of the package is to make KNN tuning more efficient and accessible for students learning statistical machine learning in R, especially for students in STATS 205 - Statistical Machine Learning at Lawrence University. Please see the Github Repo and package website (below!) for more information.

knntuner is an R package I developed for my Advanced Data Computing course. The package is designed to streamline parts of the K-nearest neighbors modeling workflow in caret by helping users create tuning grids, define cross-validation settings, and identify the best-performing value of (k).
The goal of the package is to make KNN tuning more efficient and accessible for students learning statistical machine learning in R, especially for students in STATS 205 - Statistical Machine Learning at Lawrence University. Please see the Github Repo and package website (below!) for more information.

title: My R Package: knntuner
text:
Package Purpose
K-nearest neighbors models often require repeated code for cross-validation and tuning different values of (k) when working with the caret package. knntuner helps simplify this workflow through a small set of helper functions.

title: My R Package: knntuner
text:
Main Functions

kgrid() creates a data frame of candidate (k) values for model tuning.
cv_control() creates cross-validation specifications using caret.
bestk() identifies the best-performing (k) value from a trained model.

title: My R Package: knntuner
text:
Example Workflow
The package includes a simulated student performance dataset called student_knn_data. Below, I go through a sample workflow using knntuner and its dataset student_knn_data.
In the example, make sure to run each of the code chunks in the same order that they are presented below - they represent the basic statistical machine learning workflow. Please see the vignette on the package website for more detailed information on each package function, and ways to customize their outputs.

Installation
You can install the development version of knntuner from GitHub with:
# install.packages("remotes")
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("ADC-405-S26/knntuner")


Workflow
This is a basic example which shows how knntuner can be used in the STATS 205 KNN model building and tuning workflow.

library(knntuner)
library(rsample)
library(caret)
library(recipes)
# necessary packages

In this package, there is a small simulated dataset of 100 observations in 6 variables. The data measure student characteristics, and track their performance. A head of the dataset can be seen below, and further information on each variable can be found in the vignette on the package website.

head(student_knn_data) # simulated dataset as a part of knntuner (100 observations)

  id age study_hours     score private_tutoring pass
1  1  18          12 100.00000               NO  YES
2  2  21           7  66.49531              YES   NO
3  3  18          10  82.54343              YES  YES
4  4  18           8  50.57019              YES   NO
5  5  20          12  85.38308              YES  YES
6  6  21           5  63.46618              YES   NO


First, start with the standard split of data into a training set and a test set. This example uses the student dataset built into the package.

set.seed(208)

knntuner_data_split <- initial_split(data = student_knn_data, prop = 0.8) # setting training data to be 80%, and test data to be 20%, and saving these settings as an object

student_train <- training(knntuner_data_split) # training data
student_test  <- testing(knntuner_data_split) # test data

Next, create a recipe to remove the ID column, dummy-code categorical predictors, and scale the numeric predictors for KNN, to prepare the data for analysis.

student_recipe <- recipe(pass ~ ., data = student_train) |>
  step_rm(id) |> # ID will not be used as a predictor
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> # dummy encoding nominal categorical variables
  step_center(all_numeric_predictors()) |> # normalizing numeric values step 1
  step_scale(all_numeric_predictors()) # normalizing numeric values step 2

Then, define your cross-validation specifications with the cv_control function.

cv <- cv_control() # creating the cv specifications and storing them as cv

Next, you can train and cross-validate your model using the specifications that you set. Firstly, use the kgrid function to quickly create a dataframe to hold the cross-validation results for each k value. kgrid allows you to choose the minimum and maximum k values to test, as well as the step size to take.

set.seed(208)

k_grid <- kgrid(1, 9, 2) # knntuner function here, creating the desired kgrid and storing it as an object

student_model <- train(
  student_recipe,
  data = student_train,
  method = "knn",
  trControl = cv, # knntuner object here!
  tuneGrid = k_grid, # knntuner object here!
  metric = "Sens"
)

Finally, use the bestk function to identify the best performing k value to choose for your final model! Now, you can move on to training your final model, and analyzing its performance on the test data.

bestk(student_model) # finding the optimal k value!

  k       ROC      Sens      Spec     ROCSD     SensSD    SpecSD
4 7 0.9443204 0.9277778 0.8642857 0.0415595 0.06617294 0.1014877

title: Text Analysis - How Does the BBC Frame Sports News?
text: NOTE: This project was completed jointly with Frank (Minh) Nguyen. This page highlights the sections of the project that I primarily worked on, and where we collaborated.

title: Text Analysis - How Does the BBC Frame Sports News?
text:
Overview
For this project, my partner and I used text analysis methods to examine how BBC Sport framed different sports through language and sentiment. We analyzed a dataset of BBC Sport articles from 2004 to 2005, focusing on how word choice, headline sentiment, and sport-specific vocabulary differed across categories such as football, cricket, rugby, tennis, and athletics.
The project involved cleaning raw text files, tokenizing article text, removing stop words, calculating sentiment scores, using tf-idf to identify distinctive words, and creating visualizations to interpret patterns in sports journalism.

title: Text Analysis - How Does the BBC Frame Sports News?
text:
Load Packages

# loading packages
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(fs)
library(readr)
library(stringr)

title: Text Analysis - How Does the BBC Frame Sports News?
text:
Data Wrangling

# Locate all text files in the BBC Sport dataset.
# recurse = TRUE allows R to search inside each sport category folder.
article_files <- dir_ls("bbcsport", recurse = TRUE, glob = "*.txt")

# Create one dataset where each row represents one article.
# category identifies the sport folder, article_id identifies the file,
# and text stores the full article text.
articles <- tibble(file_path = article_files) %>%
  mutate(
    category = path_file(path_dir(file_path)),
    article_id = path_file(file_path),
    text = map_chr(file_path, read_file)
  )


# Extract the headline from each article.
# The headline appears as the first line of each text file.
articles <- articles %>%
  mutate(
    headline = str_extract(text, "^[^\n]+")
  )


# Clean the article text and tokenize it into individual words.
# Numbers and extra spaces are removed before tokenization.
# Stop words are removed so the analysis focuses on more meaningful terms.
article_words <- articles %>%
  mutate(
    text_clean = str_to_lower(text),
    text_clean = str_replace_all(text_clean, "[0-9]+", " "),
    text_clean = str_replace_all(text_clean, "\\s+", " ")
  ) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text_clean) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")

title: Text Analysis - How Does the BBC Frame Sports News?
text:
Distinctive Words by Sport
To identify the words most distinctive to each sport category, I calculated tf-idf scores. A higher tf-idf score means that a word appears frequently within one sport category but is relatively uncommon across the other categories.

# Count how often each word appears in each sport category.
# bind_tf_idf() calculates the tf-idf score for each word/category pair.
sport_tfidf <- article_words %>%
  count(category, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, category, n)

# Select the 10 words with the highest tf-idf scores within each sport.
top_sport_tfidf <- sport_tfidf %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 10) %>%
  ungroup()


# Visualize the most distinctive words in each sport category.
top_sport_tfidf %>%
  mutate(word = reorder_within(word, tf_idf, category)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = tf_idf, y = word)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ category, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  labs(
    title = "Distinctive Words by BBC Sport Categories",
    subtitle = "Highest tf-idf words are frequent within one sport and relatively rare in others",
    x = "tf-idf",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








The tf-idf analysis shows that each BBC Sport category developed its own distinctive vocabulary. Football articles were strongly associated with club names and major football figures, while tennis coverage centered more heavily on individual athletes. Cricket included more technical and national terms, and rugby emphasized players, teams, and sport-specific language.

title: Text Analysis - How Does the BBC Frame Sports News?
text:
Headline Sentiment
Next, I examined the sentiment of BBC Sport headlines using the Bing sentiment lexicon. For each article headline, I calculated a sentiment score by subtracting the number of negative words from the number of positive words.

# Tokenize the article headlines into individual words.
# Stop words are removed before joining with the sentiment lexicon.
headline_words <- articles %>%
  mutate(
    headline_clean = str_to_lower(headline),
    headline_clean = str_replace_all(headline_clean, "[0-9]+", " "),
    headline_clean = str_replace_all(headline_clean, "\\s+", " ")
  ) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, headline_clean) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")


# Join headline words with the Bing sentiment lexicon.
# Count positive and negative words in each headline.
headline_sentiment <- headline_words %>%
  inner_join(get_sentiments("bing"), by = "word") %>%
  count(category, article_id, sentiment) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sentiment,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    positive = coalesce(positive, 0),
    negative = coalesce(negative, 0),
    headline_sentiment_score = positive - negative
  )


# Join the sentiment scores back to the full headline dataset.
# Headlines with no positive or negative words receive a sentiment score of 0.
headline_sentiment_full <- articles %>%
  select(category, article_id, headline) %>%
  left_join(headline_sentiment, by = c("category", "article_id")) %>%
  mutate(
    positive = coalesce(positive, 0),
    negative = coalesce(negative, 0),
    headline_sentiment_score = coalesce(headline_sentiment_score, 0)
  )


# Visualize headline sentiment scores by sport category.
ggplot(
  headline_sentiment_full,
  aes(
    x = headline_sentiment_score,
    y = reorder(category, headline_sentiment_score, median)
  )
) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.12, alpha = 0.35, size = 1.8) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    shape = 22,
    size = 4.5,
    fill = "white"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "BBC Sport Headlines Are Mostly Neutral, but Some Sports Show More Variance",
    subtitle = "Each small point represents one headline; the square is the sport average",
    x = "Headline sentiment score (positive words minus negative words)",
    y = "Sport"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








The sentiment analysis suggests that most BBC Sport headlines from 2004 to 2005 were relatively neutral, with many headlines clustering near a sentiment score of zero. However, some sports, especially football, showed wider variation in headline sentiment. This suggests that while BBC Sport maintained a professional news style, some sports still encouraged more emotionally expressive coverage and storytelling.

title: Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures
text: In my final project in my advanced data computing class, Binh Vu and I analyzed and produced a poster in R about a paper called “Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures,” which was written by Leo Breiman in 2001. We discussed how he passionately backed algorithmic modeling (he invented Random Forests!) in a statistical culture that, at the time, mainly used data modeling.

title: Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures
text: In my final project in my advanced data computing class, Binh Vu and I analyzed and produced a poster in R about a paper called “Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures,” which was written by Leo Breiman in 2001. We discussed how he passionately backed algorithmic modeling (he invented Random Forests!) in a statistical culture that, at the time, mainly used data modeling.

title: Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures
text:
Main Argument
Breiman argued that algorithmic modeling should be a significant part of a statistician’s toolbox. He believed that statisticians were choosing to use data models out of habit, rather than allowing their goals and datasets to guide their methods. He highlighted that robustness checks for data models were not as strong as they seemed, and thoughtlessly using the wrong model would lead to biased results. He suggested that, when predictive power was a higher priority than interpretability, algorithmic models would be a better choice for data scientists.

title: Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures
text:
Tradeoffs
But when a statistician decides to use an algorithmic model, they must trade away their model’s interpretability. Algorithmic models’ functions are much more complicated compared to those of straightforward data models. They treat the black box of nature as unknown, and strive to create a complicated function that emulates nature as well as possible. Data models attempt to cleanly map out the relationships within the black box of nature, and thus must inherently be more simple for human interpretation.
In this manner, choosing a method between the two cultures of data and algorithmic modeling becomes a balancing act of what to prioritize: interpretability, or prediction accuracy? The correct answer lies in the context of the problem. For example, in predicting patient outcomes, algorithmic models may be the better choice for their superior predictive ability. However, when exploring relationships, such as how age affects salary, data models likely fit the problem and the goals of the statistician better.

title: Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures
text:
Impact
Since the paper was published, algorithmic models have become more and more common, especially because the problems data scientists face have become more and more complicated. With lots of variables, weak contributing signals across many features, and highly non-linear data structures, these problems suit algorithmic models well. Breiman predicted that this would happen as the problems we face advance.
Over a quarter of a century ago, however, algorithmic models were much less common. This paper advocated for their use, and opened the door to a whole new side of data science, with new and exciting capabilities. Since then, we have seen large strides in these complex models, which have even eventually led to large language models and AI. Algorithmic models continue to be developed and explored, and likely will play a part in solving many pressing questions in this century.
